newsitem.title: CHINA: China founds 1997 HK legislature, defies Britain.
newsitem.headline: China founds 1997 HK legislature, defies Britain.

text.p: China defied British objections on Saturday and founded a new Hong Kong lawmaking body stuffed with pro-Beijing politicians.
The provisional legislature due to take over in July was founded in the frontier city of Shenzhen, opening the way for a possible clash in the World Court.
An elite of 400 rich or influential Hong Kong electors, carefully screened by Beijing, cast votes to appoint 60 legislators who will replace the current Legislative Council (Legco).

Under a blanket of heavy security, the voting was conducted in Shenzhen's City Hall in a room decked with red curtains and the red Chinese communist crest with five golden stars. The voters cast their ballots in big red envelopes.

The historic act came a day after British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind challenged China to go with Britain to the International Court of Justice in The Hague, which arbitrates treaty disputes, to get a ruling on the new body's legality.
But Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, summing up Saturday's meeting, told Britain the body was legal.

"The provisional legislature is to make some indispensable laws for post-1997 Hong Kong and will not affect Britain's governance of Hong Kong before 1997 (before the handover) and will not be a substitute for the present Legco," he said.

He said that under the handover treaty a "through train" legislature was planned but Britain had violated the treaty and understandings with China, and had derailed it, a reference to democratic reforms introduced without China's consent.
Qian said laws enacted by the provisional chamber would only come into effect after July 1, when Hong Kong becomes a quasi-autonomous Special Administrative Region of China.
China has been bent on dismantling the current elected legislature after reforms brought in by Chris Patten, Britain's last governor in Hong Kong, enlarged the democratic franchise.
"This situation, which Britain doesn't want to see, was ironically of their own making," he said.

The 60 lawmakers appointed to the provisional legislature were chosen by the same China-controlled Selection Committee that recently picked shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa as Patten's successor at the helm of the territory of 6.3 million people.
The Hong Kong public had no vote in the process.

There were 130 candidates, all carefully screened in advance. Of the winners, 33 are incumbent pro-Beijing legislators including Legco president Andrew Wong, raising the spectre that the present chamber will end up as a lame duck even before China disbands it.
Ten of Saturday's winners -- including Elsie Tu, Peggy Lam, Cheng Kai-nam, Tam Yiu-chung and Tsang Yok-sing -- were losers in Hong Kong's most democratic election to date, in September 1995.

Candidates from pro-China parties such as the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong and the Liberal Party also scored with nine and 10 seats respectively. The Progressive Alliance took five.
Dominic Chan, recently expelled from Hong Kong's Democratic Party, the favourites in the 1995 polls, also won a seat.
Qian hailed the contest as "just, fair, open and based on democratic principles" and said the result reflected Hong Kong people's views.
"The provisional legislature has representation from the business sector, labour sector and has 33 incumbent legislators ...which will enhance a stable transition," he said.
